transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-02 14:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Neill (Redwood SE), Daniel Park (Head of ML, Suncrest), Aisha Rahman (CTO, Suncrest), Mark Fletcher (Platform Eng, Suncrest)

Summary: discovery focused on dedicated GPU pools for production inference, isolation/compliance needs, burst capacity strategy and benchmark requirements. Suncrest is evaluating Dedicated vs Hosted vs private (VPC) with security as a gating factor for committing to reserved capacity.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'll kick us off. We're here to understand your production requirements and see where Redwood Dedicated could fit.
[00:18] Daniel Park: Yeah thanks Maya, appreciate it. Quick context — we run a mix of real-time scoring for our trading signals and batched overnight jobs. Latency critical for the real-time stuff, need predictable throughput, and we have pretty strict data isolation rules.
[00:35] Aisha Rahman: And from a compliance perspective we need SOC2, SSO, KMS integration, and audit logs forwarded to our SIEM.
[00:45] Liam O'Neill: Got it. That aligns with customers who go Dedicated. A few quick clarifying Qs — what does your throughput look like for realtime? tokens/sec or requests/sec?
[00:56] Mark Fletcher: For inference, 200-300 rps during market hours, spikes to 800 rps for certain events, average payload maybe 250 tokens per request. Overnight batches are heavy but less latency sensitive.
[01:14] Maya Chen: Perfect, that's helpful. With those spikes we usually recommend a reserved GPU pool sized for baseline load plus burst strategy — Dedicated supports configurable burst capacity and autoscaling policies.
[01:28] Daniel Park: Can you explain the burst model — is it pre-warmed reserved or do you leverage cloud on-demand GPUs? Concerned about cold-starts.
[01:39] Liam O'Neill: Sure — two approaches. One is reserved baseline capacity (pinned GPUs) for low-latency traffic, and a burst lane that can use either reserved spare in the pool or temporarily scale with cloud instances. For the latter, we recommend a warm pool and short scale windows to avoid cold starts, and fallback to a slightly cheaper quantized model for non-critical traffic.
[02:05] Aisha Rahman: How fast are we talking for scale up? We can't tolerate > 500ms added latency during a spike.
[02:12] Liam O'Neill: With warm pools and continuous batching, we've seen sub-second scale for in-pool burst. If we need to spin new instances, it depends on region and instance type — often 30-90s. That's why the warm pool + KV cache is important. (note: transcript sometimes hears K V cash instead of KV cache)
[02:35] Daniel Park: Okay, so we'd need to size baseline to cover normal highs, use warm pool for predictable spikes, and accept maybe limited overflow for extreme events.
[02:44] Maya Chen: Exactly. Also we can set policy-based routing — route the highest priority traffic to baseline nodes and route lower-priority to overflow or quantized variants.
[02:56] Mark Fletcher: About isolation: we must ensure customer data never touches multi-tenant storage. How does Redwood Dedicated handle that?
[03:04] Liam O'Neill: Dedicated gives you isolated GPU pools and optional private networking — VPC peering or private link. By default, the control plane is shared, but you can get a private control plane for enterprise/private deployments. Data-plane isolation ensures model artifacts and KV cache stay in your network or customer-only buckets.
[03:21] Aisha Rahman: KMS/HSM integrations? We need key rotation policies and HSM-backed keys for model encryption.
[03:28] Maya Chen: We support KMS integrations across AWS/GCP/Azure, and for Private deployments there are HSM options. We'll share our security docs.
[03:34] Daniel Park: One more — multitenancy: if we reserve GPUs, are they preemption-free? Like, can we get preemptible instances to save cost?
[03:45] Liam O'Neill: Reserved Dedicated capacity is non-preemptible. For cost savings, some customers use a mixed pool: reserved for critical workloads and preemptible or spot for non-critical batch jobs. Redwood routing keeps critical traffic off spot nodes.
[04:00] Speaker 3: (brief crosstalk)
[04:06] Daniel Park: Pricing is a big question for us — do you charge per-GPU hour plus data transfer or a flat seat for the pool?
[04:15] Maya Chen: Pricing varies — reserved monthly commits for GPU capacity plus overage rates. We provide an example pricing deck; for pilots we can do a time-limited committed pool. I'll send specific numbers after this call.
[04:28] Mark Fletcher: From an ops perspective, what's the deployment flow? CI/CD, model rollouts, canary?
[04:35] Liam O'Neill: We have rollout controls — canaries, percentage-based traffic splits, automatic rollback on error/latency regressions. Integrates with your CI so model packages can be promoted. Also token-level cost dashboards so you can see per-route cost.
[04:51] Aisha Rahman: Audit logs — can we forward to our Splunk or Datadog?
[04:55] Liam O'Neill: Yes, we can export audit logs and traces to your SIEM. We also keep immutable audit trails for compliance.
[05:05] Daniel Park: For benchmarks — what do you need from us?
[05:09] Liam O'Neill: Sample requests, QPS profile, representative prompts, and an S3 bucket or secure endpoint for us to pull logs/results. We'll run both latency and throughput tests, and try quantized vs fp16 variants if you want cost comparison.
[05:25] Maya Chen: We'll coordinate a benchmark run. For the pilot, customers typically do a 2-4 week pilot with a mid-size pool to validate SLOs.
[05:33] Daniel Park: Timeline — we're hoping to have pilot decision within 2-3 weeks, with the pilot starting mid-April if everything looks good.
[05:40] Maya Chen: Sounds achievable. We'll get pricing + security docs to you by tomorrow, and Liam will reach out to set up the benchmark harness.
[05:49] Mark Fletcher: One more technical nit — do you support model pinning to specific GPU families? We have GPU affinity for some kernels.
[05:58] Liam O'Neill: Yes, you can pin models to instance types, and we have kernel selection logic that picks optimized kernels per model/hardware. We'll note that for the benchmark.
[06:10] Aisha Rahman: Any competitors we should be aware of? We're also talking to Vertex and Bedrock for managed options. Pricing and security will be the tilt.
[06:20] Maya Chen: Totally expected. We stand out on transparent performance profiles and observability for production unit economics.
[06:28] Daniel Park: Alright, thanks.
